desc:
Write p / q in decimal as I.d1d2d3..., where I is the integer part. Return the digit dn, the n-th digit after the decimal point. Digits past the end of a terminating expansion are 0.

The expansion can be very long, so compute the digit directly instead of generating all the digits before it.

p = 1, q = 3, n = 5  -> 3
p = 1, q = 8, n = 3  -> 5
p = 22, q = 7, n = 2 -> 4   (22 / 7 = 3.142857...)
hints: Long division produces the digits one at a time. The digit at position n depends only on the remainder left after n - 1 steps.
That remainder is (p * 10n-1) mod q. Modular exponentiation computes it in O(log n) steps without producing the earlier digits.
If s is that remainder, the next digit is (10 * s) // q. Python's pow(10, n - 1, q) gives the power modulo q.
editorial: Let x = p / q. The digits after the point are fixed by the fractional part of 10n-1 x, and the nth digit is the integer part of 10 times that fractional part. Since 10n-1 p = m q + s with 0 ≤ s < q, the fractional part of 10n-1 x is exactly s / q.

So the digit is (10 * s) // q with s = (p * 10n-1) mod q. Modular exponentiation keeps every intermediate value below q squared, so a billion-sized n costs about 30 multiplications. Long division by hand gives the same digits and is useful as a brute force check.
